title: 0/1 & Unbounded Knapsack
summary: The take-or-leave-it recurrence over a weight-capacity axis — the reference case interviewers use to test whether you can reason about DP state design from scratch.

slides.markdown:
Knapsack is the problem every DP curriculum uses to teach **2D state design**: given items with weights and values and a capacity limit, pick a subset that maximizes value without exceeding the capacity.

It matters less for the specific problem than for what it teaches — a huge fraction of "pick a subset under a constraint" interview questions are knapsack wearing a costume. Subset-sum, partition-equal-subset, and coin-change-style counting problems all reduce to the same `(item, capacity)` table.

Get comfortable with this state and its space optimization here, because you'll reuse both without relabeling them for the rest of your DP career.

slides.subTitle: (item index, remaining capacity)
slides.markdown:
One index isn't enough here — the answer depends on **both** which items remain to consider and how much capacity is left. That's why knapsack needs a 2D table where 1D DP sufficed before.

`dp[i][w]` = the best value achievable using only the first `i` items with capacity `w`. At each `(i, w)`, the choice is take-or-skip item `i`:

- **Skip it**: `dp[i-1][w]` — same capacity, one fewer item considered.
- **Take it** (only if `weight[i] <= w`): `value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]]` — the capacity left after paying for it, using the items before this one.

`dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]])` when the item fits, else just `dp[i-1][w]`.

slides.subTitle: Rows as items, columns as capacity
slides.markdown:
Picture a grid with one row per item (plus a row 0 for "no items") and one column per capacity from 0 to the max. Filling proceeds row by row: row `i` reads only row `i-1`, at columns `w` and `w - weight[i]`, both already computed.

The final answer sits in the bottom-right cell, `dp[n][W]` — the best value using all `n` items with the full capacity `W`. Every other cell is a smaller, already-solved version of the same question.

slides.sectionTitle: Forward iteration reuses an item by accident
slides.markdown:
In the space-optimized 1D version of 0/1 knapsack, iterating capacity **forward** (low to high) silently allows the same item to be counted twice. Because a 1D array collapses the "previous row" and "current row" into one array, updating `dp[w]` forward means `dp[w - weight[i]]` might already reflect item `i` having been taken earlier in this same pass — the array no longer distinguishes "before considering item i" from "after."

The fix is to iterate capacity **backward** (high to low) in the 1D version: by the time you compute `dp[w]`, every smaller `dp[w - weight[i]]` you read still holds last row's value, because you haven't overwritten it yet this pass. This single loop-direction detail is the most common 0/1 knapsack bug, and it's exactly what the next slide's unbounded variant flips on purpose.

slides.subTitle: Why forward iteration becomes exactly correct
slides.markdown:
Unbounded knapsack allows unlimited copies of each item. Here, iterating capacity **forward** in the 1D array is exactly right — and it's right for the same mechanical reason forward iteration was wrong in 0/1 knapsack.

When 0/1 needed to guarantee "item `i` is used at most once," reading an already-updated `dp[w - weight[i]]` from earlier in the same pass was the bug. In the unbounded version, reusing the same item multiple times is exactly the allowed behavior — so reading a `dp[w - weight[i]]` that may already include item `i` is precisely correct, because it means "the best value using capacity `w - weight[i]`, possibly already having taken item `i` again."

One word — the reuse rule — flips one loop's direction and changes nothing else about the code shape.

| | 0/1 knapsack | Unbounded knapsack |
|---|---|---|
| Reuse | Each item at most once | Each item unlimited times |
| 1D capacity loop direction | Backward (high to low) | Forward (low to high) |
| Why | Prevents reading this pass's own update | Reading this pass's update is the intended reuse |
| 2D recurrence | `dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], v[i]+dp[i-1][w-wt[i]])` | `dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], v[i]+dp[i][w-wt[i]])` |

The 2D forms make the difference explicit too: 0/1's "take" branch reaches into row `i-1` (items before this one); unbounded's reaches into row `i` itself (this item, again). One index changes; the entire reuse semantics flips.

slides.subTitle: What divisibility buys you
slides.markdown:
Fractional knapsack — where you can take *part* of an item — has a greedy solution: sort by value-per-weight ratio and take as much of the best-ratio items as capacity allows. No DP needed.

0/1 knapsack forbids that: an item is all-or-nothing. That single divisibility rule is the entire reason one version needs DP and the other doesn't. With fractions allowed, a locally-best partial choice never needs to be revisited — you can always top off with a slice of the next-best item. Without fractions, taking a high-ratio item might leave capacity that no other item fits exactly, so the greedy choice can strand value that a different combination would have captured. That's the general lesson `greedy-vs-dp` covers in more depth: **divisibility (or, more generally, revisability) of choices is often the tell for whether greedy suffices.**

Subset-sum ("is there a subset summing to exactly `T`?") and partition-equal-subset-sum ("can the array split into two equal-sum halves?") are 0/1 knapsack with the values dropped — every item's "value" is irrelevant, only reachability matters.

`dp[i][s]` becomes a boolean: **is sum `s` reachable using the first `i` items?** The recurrence is the same take-or-skip shape: `dp[i][s] = dp[i-1][s] OR (s >= weight[i] AND dp[i-1][s - weight[i]])`. Partition-equal-subset-sum is exactly this with `T = total_sum / 2` (immediately impossible if the total is odd).

Recognizing this reduction is worth real interview points — a candidate who says "this is knapsack with the value axis collapsed to a boolean" signals real understanding of the state shape, not just memorized code for one named problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Not everything that looks like a subset problem is knapsack
slides.markdown:
"Pick a subset under a constraint" is a huge category, and knapsack only covers the slice where items are independent, order doesn't matter, and reuse rules are simple (once, unlimited, or a small fixed count). Forcing a knapsack shape onto a problem that violates those assumptions produces a recurrence that looks plausible and is wrong.

Watch for: **order-dependent subsets** (picking a subsequence where relative order matters is closer to LIS or LCS territory), **pairwise interactions between chosen items** (if item A's value depends on whether item B was also chosen, the take-or-skip independence breaks), and **combinatorial reuse rules** ("at most 2 of any item" needs a widened but still-knapsack-shaped state, not a fundamentally different one — don't over-generalize the pitfall).

The check before committing to knapsack: confirm each item's contribution is independent of which other items get picked.

The filled table gives the best *value*, not the items that produced it. To recover the selection, walk backward from `dp[n][capacity]`: at each `(i, w)`, check whether `dp[i][w] == dp[i-1][w]`. If so, item `i` wasn't used — move to `(i-1, w)`. If not, item `i` was used — record it and move to `(i-1, w - weight[i])`.

This walk-back only works cleanly on the full 2D table, because the space-optimized 1D version overwrites the history needed to distinguish "used" from "not used" at a given capacity. If you know you'll need to reconstruct the selection, keep the 2D table (or a parallel `choice[i][w]` array) rather than collapsing to 1D — the space optimization and the reconstruction requirement are in direct tension.
